'''Amikam Aharoni''' ({{langx|he|עמיקם אַהֲרֹֹנִי}}; 5 August 1929{{snd}}21 January 2002) was an Israeli [[physicist]] who has made numerous contributions to the fields of [[magnetism]]. He is the author of over a hundred works,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Amikam Aharoni |url=https://www.weizmann.ac.il/physics/eulogy/amikam-aharoni |access-date=2024-09-29 |website=www.weizmann.ac.il |language=en-GB |department=Faculty of Physics}}</ref> with his research of [[ferromagnetism]] being most accredited.<ref name="Memoriam" />

==Education==
Born in [[Safed]], Aharoni received a M.A. in [[physics]] from [[Hebrew University]] in 1953 and a Ph.D. in [[physics]] from the [[Weizmann Institute]] in 1957. His thesis was on magnetoresistive memory elements. His postdoc work with [[John Bardeen]] took him to the [[University of Illinois]] during 1958-1959. In 1971-1972, 1977–1978, and 1992 he was a senior research fellow in the Department of Metallurgy at the [[University of Oxford]]. In 1972 he was promoted to professor in the Department of Electronics at [[Weizmann Institute]], and in 1978 he was appointed the Richard Kronstein Professor of Theoretical [[Magnetism]].

==Research==
{{Expand section|date=July 2023}}

His research significantly advanced the theoretical understanding of magnetic phenomena.

Aharoni's work on micromagnetics and the phenomenological theory of ferromagnets provided deep insights into the behavior of magnetic materials<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Aharoni |first=Amikam |date=1989-09-01 |title=Micromagnetics and the phenomenological theory of ferromagnets |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevB.40.4607 |journal=Physical Review B |language=en |volume=40 |issue=7 |pages=4607–4608 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.40.4607 |issn=0163-1829|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Aharoni's 1996 book, "Introduction to the Theory of Ferromagnetism" has been described as an authoritative introduction to [[micromagnetism]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Arrott |first=Anthony |author-link=Anthony Schuyler Arrott |date=1997-09-01 |title=Book Review: Introduction to the Theory of Ferromagnetism |journal=Physics Today |publisher=AIP Publishing |volume=50 |issue=9 |pages=66–68 |doi=10.1063/1.881916 |issn=0031-9228}}</ref>

==Private life==
Aharoni's mother was a school teacher, and third-generation Israeli. His father was a teacher of mathematics (and distinguished chess master) who had emigrated from Russia, arriving in Israel in 1920. The family was religious, and Aharoni was able to recite from memory passages from both the bible and the talmud of considerable length.<ref name="Memoriam">{{Cite journal |last=Arrott |first=A. S. |year=2002 |title=In memoriam Amikam Aharoni [1929-2002] |journal=IEEE Transactions on Magnetics |volume=38 |issue=6 |pages=3577–3578 |bibcode=2002ITM....38.3577A |doi=10.1109/TMAG.2002.805685}}</ref>

In 1947, Aharoni's studies were disrupted by [[1947–1948_civil_war_in_Mandatory_Palestine|Israel's War of Independence]]. Aharoni joined the "Students' Brigade" and was deployed in and around Jerusalem, taking part in numerous actions during [[Battle_for_Jerusalem|the city's 1947–1948 siege]].<ref name="Memoriam" />

At the [[Weizmann Institute]], Aharoni met his wife Henia, and the two were married in 1955. The couple had three sons and, in time, nine grandchildren. Aharoni formally retired in 1994.<ref name="Memoriam" />

==Awards==
Distinguished Lecturer of the [[IEEE]] Magnetics Society of 1993.
